patient.chief_complaint: Progressive behavioral changes, apathy, and social withdrawal over 18 months, referred for neurological evaluation after psychiatrist noted insufficient response to antidepressants.
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. D. is a 54-year-old right-handed White male with a history of treated depression who presents for outpatient neurological evaluation at his psychiatrist's referral. Approximately 18 months ago, his wife first noticed that he seemed emotionally flat and detached from the family. Initially attributed to work stress, these changes have progressively worsened. She describes him as having lost his previously warm and engaged personality — he no longer initiates conversations, rarely asks about the children, and sits for hours watching television without reacting. More concerning, he has made several socially inappropriate comments in public settings, including making off-color remarks to neighbors and laughing at a funeral. He has developed a preference for the same television programs on repeat, and insists on eating the same meals each day. His personal hygiene has deteriorated; he requires prompting to shower.

His psychiatrist diagnosed major depressive disorder 3 years ago and initiated sertraline, which was uptitrated to 100 mg without meaningful benefit for these behavioral symptoms. He has had two psychotherapy trials without improvement. He denies depressed mood and reports feeling 'fine.' He has not had episodes of mania, psychosis, or substance use. He was placed on medical leave from his financial analyst position 18 months ago after colleagues noted errors in spreadsheets and difficulty managing complex accounts. His wife is particularly alarmed because his father underwent similar behavioral changes starting in his mid-50s and was diagnosed with dementia. Genetic testing of the father was never performed. His brother is currently being evaluated at another hospital for similar personality changes at age 51.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) due to C9orf72 repeat expansion

differential.key_features: Poor sertraline response, lack of subjective distress, behavioral features atypical for depression, positive family history of dementia, FAB and social cognition deficits
Amyloid PET negative, CSF Abeta42 normal, tau PET negative, episodic memory relatively preserved, frontal-predominant atrophy
Onset >40, progressive course, neuropsychological deficits, family history of similar neurodegenerative disease, FDG-PET abnormal
CSF 14-3-3 negative, no rapid progression to date, no myoclonus, no DWI cortical ribboning on MRI
No gait apraxia, no urinary incontinence, ventricles normal in size on MRI

critical_actions: Obtain FDG-PET and amyloid PET — MRI alone is insufficient and non-diagnostic in this case
Order C9orf72 genetic panel given family history spanning two generations
Do not attribute behavioral syndrome to depression without ruling out neurodegenerative disease — sertraline non-response is a red flag
Arrange genetic counseling — C9orf72 expansion has 50% transmission risk to children and siblings
Monitor for signs of ALS (fasciculations, dysarthria, dysphagia) given C9orf72 expansion
contraindicated_actions: Do not escalate antidepressants or antipsychotics as primary management without neurological workup
Do not reassure patient and family as 'depression' or 'personality disorder' without comprehensive neurological evaluation
Do not initiate acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) — no benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral agitation
Avoid prescribing high-dose benzodiazepines for behavioral management without specialist input
key_reasoning_points: MRI can be NORMAL or show only minimal frontal atrophy in early bvFTD, especially in C9orf72 carriers — a 'normal' or borderline MRI does NOT exclude FTD

The critical diagnostic clue is the combination of: (1) normal amyloid PET excluding AD, (2) abnormal FDG-PET showing frontal hypometabolism, (3) severe social cognition/executive deficits on neuropsychological testing, and (4) strong multigenerational family history
C9orf72 is the most common genetic cause of both familial FTD and ALS — always screen for motor neuron disease signs at follow-up

Misattribution to depression is the most common diagnostic error in young-onset bvFTD — the key differentiating features are lack of subjective mood complaints, executive and social cognition deficits, and progressive course
The sibling under evaluation at another institution likely has the same C9orf72 expansion — urgent family communication and genetic counseling is required
CSF biomarker profile (normal Abeta42, normal tau/p-tau) confirms non-Alzheimer pathology and provides additional diagnostic support
